chapter_theme: One song at Thiruvavaduthurai (திருவாவடுதுறை): the poet confesses that instead of praising Murugan he sank into courtesans and then into flattering wicked rich men in verse to escape poverty, and asks not to be left to that weariness.

848.reading: The poet confesses that, failing to praise Murugan without a slip of speech, he whirled in the pot of birth, delighted in the way of the seed and set his mind on the coral lips of price-women, then went to evil, cruel men of the earth, set them in verse as a kalpaka king of wealth and an Arjuna in battle, and recited his learning loudly to end his poverty; he asks whether Murugan will let him be worn out by this fancy, empty-handed and confused. The praise tells of Krishna who trampled the hooded serpent, tore the crocodile that seized the elephant and drank the breast of the deceiving demoness until she died, and of Rama, and describes the peacock adorned with gold and gems, at Thiruvavaduthurai.
848.nuance: The confession is double: the courtesans, and the court poet's trade, praising துற்சனர் (the wicked) as கற்பக ராசன் and அர்ச்சுனன் for money. The proper object of praise (உனைக் கனக்கத் துதித்து) is set against the false one. The praise of the peacock's jewelled trappings is hard to divide.

links.note: Both confess praising unworthy men as the kalpaka tree and as Arjuna to get money; 848 sets that trade beside the courtesans as two forms of one failure to praise Murugan.
